# A message queue as an extension

[pgmq](https://github.com/pgmq/pgmq) gives Postgres a queue in the style of Amazon SQS, written in
plain SQL. Reading a message hides it for a number of seconds instead of locking it, so a message
whose consumer crashes reappears. In the lab, a message read with a 2 second timeout by a consumer that then died came back 2.2 seconds
later with `read_ct` 2. Every operation is a SQL function, so anything that can run SQL can send or
receive, from psql to a trigger to a Go service.

## Visibility timeout

`read` moves the message's `vt` timestamp into the future, and until that moment no other reader
sees it. A queue's whole life takes four calls:

```sql
SELECT pgmq.create('jobs');
SELECT pgmq.send('jobs', '{"page": "orm/quickstart"}');
SELECT msg_id, read_ct, message FROM pgmq.read('jobs', 30, 1);   -- hidden for 30 s
SELECT pgmq.archive('jobs', 1);                                  -- done: moved to pgmq.a_jobs
```

A consumer that finishes its work deletes or archives the message, and one that crashes does
nothing at all. When `vt` passes the message is visible again, with `read_ct` counting the new
attempt.

## Delivery guarantees

Delivery is at least once, so a message can reach more than one consumer. pgmq cannot tell a slow consumer from a crashed one, so long
work must call `set_vt` to extend its lease (the time it keeps the message hidden). In the notebook,
a 3 second job on a 2 second timeout loses its message to a second consumer, and the same job keeps
it when it extends the lease every half second.

`pop` reads and deletes a message in one statement, which gives at-most-once delivery instead. A
message that a consumer pops and then fails on is gone.

## Retries

pgmq has no retry policy of its own, but `read_ct` and `set_vt` are enough to write one:

```python
for msg_id, read_ct, message in read_batch():
    try:
        handle(message)
        archive(msg_id)
    except Exception:
        if read_ct >= 3:
            with conn.transaction():       # in exactly one of the two queues, always
                send("jobs_dead", message)
                delete("jobs", msg_id)
        else:
            set_vt(msg_id, 2 ** read_ct)  # backoff
```

The notebook runs this loop against a flaky page and a broken one. The flaky page succeeds on its
second attempt, and the broken one lands in the dead-letter queue after its third.

## Consumers and notifications

`read` claims messages with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` inside one `UPDATE`, so four threads reading
400 messages took exactly 100 each, none twice, in 0.12 s. Consumers can wait inside Postgres with
`read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` adds a trigger that sends `NOTIFY` on
`pgmq.q_<name>.INSERT`. From send to receipt, NOTIFY took about 12 ms (median of 8), while polling
took up to its interval.

pgmq also has:

- delayed messages, where `send(queue, msg, delay)` sets `vt` in the future at insert time
- FIFO groups, where messages with the same `x-pgmq-group` header come out of `read_grouped` in
  order, one at a time (a plain `read` ignores groups, so every consumer of that queue has to use
  the grouped functions)
- topics, where `bind_topic('orders.*.paid', 'payments')` and `send_topic('orders.eu.paid', msg)`
  route messages with RabbitMQ-style wildcards, `*` matching one word and `#` any number of words
  after a dot
- archive tables, `pgmq.a_<name>`, which keep every archived message with its `archived_at` time

## pgmq and pgqueuer compared

Both claim work with `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, and neither holds a lock while the work runs. They
differ in how a claim expires and in where the logic lives. In pgmq the claim is a timestamp that
the consumer must keep pushing forward. In pgqueuer it is a `picked` status, and the library keeps
the worker's heartbeat fresh for you.

| | pgmq | pgqueuer |
|---|---|---|
| what it is | a Postgres extension, SQL functions | a Python library over plain tables |
| a claim | `read` pushes `vt` ahead | dequeue sets `status = 'picked'` |
| a claim expires | when `vt` passes, unless the consumer calls `set_vt` | when the worker's heartbeat is older than `heartbeat_timeout`, refreshed for you |
| consumers | any language with a Postgres driver | Python asyncio workers |
| waking up | `read_with_poll`, or `enable_notify_insert` and `LISTEN` | `LISTEN ch_pgqueuer`, always on |
| retries | by hand, from `read_ct` and `set_vt` | built in, with `on_failure="hold"` |
| extras | archive, topics, FIFO groups, partitioned queues | dedupe keys, fleet-wide limits, cron schedules |

pgmq suits a queue that several languages or services share, or one fed from SQL itself, where an
SQS-shaped API is the point. pgqueuer suits a Python application that wants a worker framework with
retries, limits and schedules already written.
